name: Daria Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Daria, 58, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes lending software for public libraries. I have a bachelor’s degree and know the usual loan and return problems well enough to solve them without much fuss. I follow the item record, compare the desk receipt and talk with a librarian when a fine is wrong. I have never used AI tools; a borrower’s history should not become a test prompt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are work and money at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Joel repairs lifts for a building contractor, and our children are grown. My pay is typical for a developer, his hours are steady, and we have a mortgage with about four months of expenses saved. There are some other software jobs nearby. Retirement is coming into view, but we have not checked actual income statements to see when it is possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell librarians AI Plateau still leaves someone answerable when a returned book shows as overdue. A receipt in a reader’s hand ought to count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think both wages and our mortgage are secure in this picture. Four months saved gives us time to handle a household repair while I keep the job I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking loan records against desk receipts with a librarian before changing fine code. I’d continue saving 180 monthly while both wages hold. In the first year I’d keep borrower histories out of AI tools entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own pay and bills. I am glad the librarian can still correct a wrong fine with a person on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which return receipt changed the code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A child returned a book on Saturday, but the overnight batch ran on Monday and charged a fine. I found the receipt and fixed the date rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel and I would keep our ordinary weekend outings. We would not set a retirement date from a neighbour’s pension story.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking library fines.
I would use **desk receipts** before changing return dates.
think: I expect **both wages** to stay secure while librarians still need receipt checks.
Our **four-month reserve** covers ordinary household repairs without missing the mortgage.
do: **Match** loan records with desk receipts and librarian review.
**Keep** borrower histories out of AI tools.
feel: **Calm** about work and mortgage, pleased with human correction.
S0.quote: A receipt in a reader’s hand ought to count for something.
fieldNote: Her **manual receipt check** and librarian conversation guide code fixes when a returned book is wrongly fined.
Two steady wages and **four months saved** make the mild world secure while she keeps the familiar job.

steps.text: Keep checking library fines against desk receipts with librarian review
Save 180 monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check lending code, but borrowers still need a person to challenge a fine. I would ask our union to insist on a named librarian for disputed charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think management could remove some mid-level testing hours, including mine. I have four months saved, but I do not want to spend it while a new system quietly changes the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the workplace union’s library group and bring four anonymous wrong-fine cases. I’d ask management to publish how many fines were reversed after automated decisions. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d search actual local support posts with written wages that, with Joel’s usual pay, cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, with enough savings to search carefully. I do not want a borrowed book to become a debt because no one owns the appeal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you bring to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One borrower had two editions with the same short title and the wrong item was charged. I would bring the case without their name to the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Joel’s work be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel’s lift repairs are hands-on and may change later, but the scheduling is screen work. We would count his current paid hours, not promise a future overtime rota.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach lending code before lift-repair robots.
I would demand **named fine appeals** for borrowers.
think: I expect my **testing hours** might shrink.
I know **four months saved** permits a search but not an endless one.
do: **Join** union library group with four anonymous fine cases.
**Search** real support posts with mortgage-covering written wages if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about possible reduced hours, with time to search.
S1.quote: I do not want a borrowed book to become a debt because no one owns the appeal.
fieldNote: Her **union action** uses anonymous wrong-fine cases and reversal counts.
She will move only for **real stated pay** sufficient with Joel’s usual wage if her hours fall.

steps.text: Join union library group with four anonymous fine cases and seek reversal counts
Search real support posts if hours fall only with written pay covering mortgage alongside Joel’s wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches lending code in 2028, with hands-on lift robots around 2031. Joel’s scheduling may change earlier than his visits to broken lifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer post could disappear. Four months saved gives us a bridge. There may not be another local coding job after AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our union to bargain as a group for written layoff terms and a borrower appeal route. I’d hold our savings for mortgage bills and call the lender early if my pay stops. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to actual paid openings and eligible public income help rather than count our grown children’s wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my pay, though I can plan for several months. I would lie awake if the library fine system kept running with no one to answer a reader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the bills are ours to handle. If we needed family help later, I would ask only after checking whether they can spare it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could lift work support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel would keep lift work while paid calls exist. We would not call it safe forever because the robots are three years later.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach lending code before 2031 lift robots.
I would demand **borrower appeals** after software staff cuts.
think: I expect my **developer post** could disappear when full thinking AI reaches library software.
I cannot assume **local code jobs** survive full thinking AI at other firms.
do: **Bargain** with union for written layoff terms and borrower appeals.
**Hold** savings for mortgage and call lender early if pay stops.
**Apply** to actual paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about wage loss and reader appeals.
S2.quote: There may not be another local coding job after AGI by 2028.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 code loss**, while lift-repair robots follow around 2031.
A **four-month reserve** buys a bridge, while union demands and eligible help stay conditional.

steps.text: Bargain through union for written layoff terms and borrower appeals
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches lending code in 2031 and lift robots around 2034. Five years lets me check whether another employer will pay for my library knowledge while coding posts still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think my current post could end. I do not want to learn an untested tool at 58 for a job that might vanish anyway, but a real offer before 2031 could improve our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask two nearby library-software firms for actual vacancies and written pay, and compare their hours and travel with my current job. I’d change employers only with a signed offer that raises net household income without losing paid weeks or health cover. In the first year after 2031, if code work ends, I’d seek real paid openings and use savings for bills; I would not assume the new firm is protected from AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about code work, with time to verify another employer. A higher salary on paper is no help if the commute and lost weeks eat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a vacancy need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the hiring manager who speaks to librarians about disputed fines. I would not leave a job I know for a vacancy that only promises a higher title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare household pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel and I would compare the signed pay packet with the mortgage and actual travel. Our children’s pay would stay off the sheet.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 lift robots.
I would seek **verified higher pay** while coding employers still hire.
think: I expect my **current post** could end when AGI reaches library code in 2031.
I cannot assume **another software firm** survives full 2031 AGI after a job switch.
do: **Ask** two library-software firms about actual vacancies, written pay, hours and travel.
**Move jobs** only with signed net gain, no lost paid weeks or health cover.
**Seek** real paid work if code ends after 2031, using savings for bills.
feel: **Anxious** about code work, with time to verify offers.
S3.quote: A higher salary on paper is no help if the commute and lost weeks eat it.
fieldNote: She uses the **five-year lead** to compare actual library employers without claiming a safe refuge after AGI.
Her **switching gate** needs signed pay, net gain, continuous paid weeks and health cover.

steps.text: Change library-software firms only with signed net gain, continuous paid weeks and health cover
Seek real paid openings if code work ends after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches lending code in 2036; hands-on lift robots follow around 2039. A decade gives workers time to demand paid transitions and check actual retirement resources.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my wage is steady now, but middle-level testing hours may shrink before 2036. Four months saved is not a retirement plan, and I will not assume a pension covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking fine records against receipts and save 180 monthly while both wages hold. I’d ask our union each year for numbers on paid jobs and borrower appeals. In the first year after 2036, if code ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if written income, savings and mortgage figures show we can pay ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later job changes, with current wages and housing secure. I want evidence before either leaving work or naming a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request statements from our own retirement providers and compare them with the mortgage balance. My neighbour’s retirement age tells me nothing about our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the union measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the union one clear wrong-fine case each year without the reader’s name. A count of corrected fines is better than an AI demonstration.

I would demand **paid transitions** and borrower-appeal figures.
think: I expect my **wage** to hold in the near term.
I worry **testing hours** could shrink before 2036.
do: **Keep** checking fine receipts and save 180 while both wages hold.
**Ask** union yearly for paid-job and appeal figures.
**Seek** real paid work if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Uneasy** about future cuts, with current household pay secure.
S4.quote: My neighbour’s retirement age tells me nothing about our account.
fieldNote: Her **union record** measures paid work and corrected fines each year, rather than accepting AI demonstrations as proof.
Retirement needs **written household figures** compared with the mortgage, with no assumed pension or children’s wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because four months saved is a bridge, not a job. Written layoff terms, a human borrower appeal route, eligible income help and real paid work would help. I would not ask the children to fund our mortgage without checking their own situation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the librarian what happens when the return receipt and the fine disagree. A computer can charge a reader faster than it can listen.

headlineQuote: A computer can charge a reader faster than it can listen.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and four months saved.
She has **never used AI** and checks library fines against receipts and librarian explanations.
Her partner’s **lift-repair pay** is steady, so current income is secure despite future code exposure.
She pursues **union appeal rights** and a signed net-improving job only while real coding employers hire.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove code work with only four months to find income.
whatWouldHelp: **Written layoff terms**, borrower appeals, eligible help and real paid work would help.
